proposed_edges.relationship: In his article's abstract, challenges not the conclusion that upper Great Lakes fur-trade settlements were Métis but 'how they are ethnohistorically imagined as such', and appeals for a Métis 'counter-ethnohistory' anchored 'in an analytics of peoplehood' (2011, abstract)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Abstract only, Andersen, Ethnohistory 58:1 (2011): the article examines how 'contemporary ethnohistorians examining upper Great Lakes fur trade settlements' handle 'the racialized logics governing the retrofitting of these settlements as “métis” and “Métis”' and 'the recent creep of juridical logics into ethnohistorical conversations'; 'Rather than challenging ethnohistorical conclusions that these settlements were/are Métis, this article challenges how they are ethnohistorically imagined as such'. His book (2014, p. 13, read) says chapter 2 explores 'the Powley decision's effects on government policy making and on upper Great Lakes ethnohistory'. The article body and chapter 2 are unread, and no ethnohistorian is named in the passages read, so the arrow goes to the field. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Finds 'the undertheorization of identity sitting at the heart of scholarship on the Canadian politics of recognition': Taylor's use of 'identity' conceals a tension between 'situated self-understanding' and 'official classification' (2014)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 'Métis' (2014), introduction p. 14 (publisher sample, read), summarising chapter 5: two 'methodological shortcomings of Taylor's narrow use of identity': it 'marginalizes discussion of the extent to which the process of public recognition itself may prove constitutive to the claims of collective identity', and 'in positioning misrecognition as an external force, it overlooks how it also shapes the internal claims of the group'. Chapter 5 itself is unread. Distinct from Coulthard's critique of Taylor (edge_2132): Andersen keeps the concept of (mis)recognition (p. 20) and criticises Taylor's concept of identity. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Andersen uses (mis)recognition 'in keeping with my own Bourdieuvian tendencies': racialized categories 'rooted in colonial structures and practices, are seen and understood as natural' (2014)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words, 'Métis' (2014), introduction p. 20 (publisher sample, read); the sample ends partway through his definition, which quotes Bourdieu. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Coulthard grounds his place-based critique in God Is Red: Deloria's 'distinction between Indigenous place-based and Western time-oriented understandings of the world' (2009)
proposed_edges.map_label: God Is Red: place against time, 2009
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Coulthard's dissertation (2009), p. 88 (read): Deloria's 'groundbreaking 1972 text, God is Red' holds that Western societies derive meaning 'in historical/developmental terms, thereby placing time as the narrative of central importance'; the quoted distinction is Coulthard's own wording; p. 89: land as a field of 'relationships of things to each other' (quoting Deloria 2001). The passage that follows, on Dene relations to land, is community knowledge and is not used (OCAP). Whether the 2014 book keeps this reading is unchecked. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Coulthard reads Adams as the writer Fanon 'most influenced' and takes from him that Indigenous 'cultural self-empowerment can be captured or co-opted by the state apparatus and directed toward neo-colonial ends' (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Coulthard's dissertation (2009), pp. 188–194 (read): p. 188, Fanon 'most influenced the work of the late … historian and Red Power activist Howard Adams'; p. 193, 'There are a number of insights to be gleaned from Adams' engagement with the work of Fanon', first the co-optation quoted above, which he applies to the 1970s Dene movement; p. 194, Adams's call to revive traditions that empower and discard those that oppress, applied to Indigenous women's struggle against the Indian Act's patriarchal legacy. The biographical and autobiographical passages on pp. 188–190 are not used (OCAP). Whether the 2014 book keeps this reading is unchecked. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Coulthard takes from Canadian historians and geographers, citing Harris, that after the waves of settlement (1860–1914) colonial development 'required first and foremost land, and only secondarily' Indigenous labour: the historical ground of 'dispossession, not proletarianization' (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Coulthard's dissertation (2009), p. 18 (read): 'It is now generally acknowledged among Canadian historians and political economists' that Native labour became 'increasingly (although by no means entirely) superfluous'; n. 48 cites Harris, 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess?' (2004), p. 167, for the land-over-labour claim; n. 47 also cites Lutz, Makuk (2008), 'On the importance of Native labour'. Restated in the conclusion, p. 215: 'as most political economists and historians have now recognized'. A use, not a critique. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)
